extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory; literature teachers; general readers interested in criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the principles, variations, and methodological implications of reader-response criticism — a school of literary theory that foregrounds the reader's experience and interpretive activity in creating textual meaning. Useful as an orientation for critics, teachers, and researchers applying reader-centered approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the reader and their experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader-response criticism is a school of literary theory that focuses on the reader (or 'audience') and their experience of a literary work, in contrast to theories that focus primarily on the author, content, or form of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate interpretations by attending to how individual readers experience the text rather than privileging authorial intention or purely textual formal features; consider the reader's emotional and cognitive engagement as central to meaning-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective response as legitimate critical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: This movement ... argues that affective response is a legitimate point for departure in criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat emotional reactions (pathos, suspense, curiosity, surprise, etc.) as valid starting points and data for critical analysis; consider empirical work on emotions in reading (e.g., studies of suspense and heart rate variability) when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader as active agent who completes meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Reader-response theory recognizes the reader as an active agent who imparts 'real existence' to the work and completes its meaning through interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should show how readers 'realize' or 'complete' texts; credit reader activity (inference, filling gaps, imagination) as constitutive of the work's meaning rather than merely responsive to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for textual and cultural constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach avoids subjectivity or essentialism in descriptions produced through its recognition that reading is determined by textual and also cultural constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reader-response work balances reader subjectivity with the constraints imposed by the text and by cultural context; avoid unbounded subjectivism by showing how the text and culture shape possible readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transactional model: text–reader transaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Transactional reader-response theory ... involves a transaction between the text's inferred meaning and the individual interpretation by the reader influenced by their personal emotions and knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating readings, analyze the dynamic exchange between textual features and the reader's background, emotions, and knowledge — how each modifies the other in producing meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective stylistics: meaning arises in reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Affective stylistics ... believe that a text can only come into existence as it is read; therefore, a text cannot have meaning independent of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus analysis on language-in-use and moment-by-moment readers' responses (literary stylistic effects) rather than assuming an independent, stable textual meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective approach: center individual responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective reader-response theory ... looks entirely to the reader's response for literary meaning as individual written responses to a text are then compared to other individual interpretations to find continuity of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and compare written individual responses; priority is given to readers' subjective accounts as the basis for literary meaning (useful in classroom or qualitative studies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological approach: readers' motives shape reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychological reader-response theory ... believes that a reader's motives heavily affect how they read, and subsequently use this reading to analyze the psychological response of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate psychological theories (e.g., psychoanalytic models, identity themes) to explain why particular readers interpret texts as they do; consider motive, defense mechanisms, and identity-based reading styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/interpretive-community approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Social reader-response theory ... states that any individual interpretation of a text is created in an interpretive community of minds consisting of participants who share a specific reading and interpretation strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate interpretations in terms of the interpretive communities (professional, pedagogical, cultural) that produce shared reading strategies; trace how communal norms shape what readings are available or authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualist vs uniformist distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative way of organizing ...: those who focus upon the individual reader's experience ('individualists') and those who assume a fairly uniform response by all readers called 'uniformists'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position analytical claims on a spectrum: do you treat responses as essentially individual (emphasize variation) or as predictable/uniform (emphasize patterns)? Explicitly justify which model you adopt and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolization and resymbolization processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The symbolization and resymbolization process consists of how an individual's personal emotions, needs and life experiences affect how a reader engages with a text; marginally altering the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using individualist frameworks, trace how personal histories and needs shape symbolic readings; use recorded or written responses (as in classroom studies) to reveal these processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental methods for measuring responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimenters ... conduct psychological experiments on a defined set of readers ... often involve participants free associating during the study, with the experimenters collecting and interpreting reader-responses in an informal way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply empirical methods (questionnaires, free association, physiological measures) to document reader responses; use standardized instruments and established experimental designs where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied reader and the text's control (Iser)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wolfgang Iser ... posits an implied reader, who is the reader a given literary work requires. The reader's activities are confined within limits set by the literary work; the reader fills in 'gaps' or areas of 'indeterminacy' of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how textual structures (gaps, indeterminacies, anticipations) guide reader responses and instantiate an 'implied reader'; show how expectation, frustration, retrospection, and reconceptualization operate in reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizon of expectations (Jauss)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hans‑Robert Jauss ... defined literature as a dialectic process of production and reception ... readers have a certain mental set, a 'horizon' of expectations ... from which perspective each reader, at any given time in history, reads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate readings historically: explicate the reader's horizon of expectations (historical norms, genres, conventions) and how texts challenge or fulfil them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical principle: avoid imposing 'proper' reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Louise Rosenblatt ... argued that it is important for the teacher to avoid imposing any 'preconceived notions about the proper way to react to any work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In teaching literature, privilege student responses and refrain from enforcing a single 'correct' interpretation; use reader-response activities (anonymous writing, seminar sharing) to surface diverse engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing objections: show how text expands reader understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: One objection ... is that it fails to account for the text being able to expand the reader's understanding. While readers can and do put their own ideas and experiences into a work, they are at the same time gaining new understanding through the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengthen reader-centered analyses by demonstrating reciprocal effects: not only how readers shape meaning but also how texts transform readers' knowledge, perspectives, or emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary/empirical extension (cognitive/neuroscience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because it rests on psychological principles, a reader-response approach readily generalizes to other arts ... cognitive psychology, psycholinguistics, neuroscience, and neuropsychoanalysis have given reader-response critics powerful and detailed models for the aesthetic process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where relevant, draw on cognitive science, psycholinguistics, and neuroscience (e.g., studies of heart rate variability, amygdala activation) to underpin claims about readers' emotional and cognitive processes.
